title: If and then
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: idhā and law both take the PAST behind them, whatever the English says. idhā dhahabtu is "if I go" and law dhahabtu is "if I had gone" — the same verb shape twice, and the particle in front is what fixes the time. Reaching for the present after idhā is the first mistake an English speaker makes here.

The split between them is real and not a matter of style. idhā is for what may well happen: idhā dhahabtu ilā as-sūq, sa-ashtarī al-khubz — the shopping is still open. law is for what did not: law dhahabtu ilā al-maṭʿam, la-akaltu as-samak — the dinner never took place. English says "if" for both and leans on its verb tenses to tell them apart; Arabic tells you in the first word.

law is L2-M1's word, not a new one. You met it in law samaḥta, "if you please", and it is the same "if" doing its ordinary job. A learner who filed it away as half of a polite phrase will not recognise it here, which is the only difficulty in it.

law's answer clause wears la- on the front of it: la-akaltu, la-kuntu, la-akalnā. That one letter is the whole of Arabic's conditional — there is no separate mood to learn and nothing to conjugate, which is a real relief: the Romance languages spend a chapter on what Arabic spends a prefix on.

lam is the negative past, and it is a particle standing in front of a PRESENT-shaped verb: lam adhhab, "I didn't go". The verb it holds is in the jussive, which this course writes exactly like the ordinary present for a sound verb — adhhab stays adhhab — and shortens for a hollow one: akūn becomes akun, anām becomes anam. That shortening is the only place the mood can be seen, and it is the only job the jussive is opened for here. The mood itself is L4's.

"Don't go" is lā plus that same jussive: lā tadhhab to a man, lā tadhhabī to a woman. It is NOT the imperative with a negative in front — L2-M4's idhhab has no negative form at all — so lā idhhab, the shape English leads you to, does not exist in Arabic.

Advice needs no new grammar. L3-M2's yajibu an and min al-afḍal an are both impersonal frames with L1-M3's an behind them, and the person turns up only in the verb at the far end. an takes the subjunctive and never shortens — yajibu an tanām, with the ā kept — which is exactly what lam does not do.

sentences.display: idhā dhahabtu ilā as-sūq, sa-ashtarī al-khubz
sentences.script: إذا ذهبت إلى السوق، سأشتري الخبز
sentences.cue: If I go to the market, I'll buy the bread
sentences.literal: If I-went to the-market, I-will-buy the-bread

words.note: "If", for what is still open. The verb behind it is PAST whatever the English says: idhā dhahabtu is "if I go", not "if I went".

sentences.trap: English puts a present after "if" — if I go. Arabic puts a past there and means the future by it, so dhahabtu behind idhā is not a report about yesterday.
sentences.sound: i-DHAA dha-HAB-tu — idhā ends on a long -ā that runs straight into the verb, with no pause between the two.

variations.display: idhā dhahabtu ilā al-maṭʿam, sa-ākul as-samak
variations.script: إذا ذهبت إلى المطعم، سآكل السمك
variations.cue: If I go to the restaurant, I'll eat the fish
variations.changed: where and what: the market becomes the restaurant, buying becomes eating

variations.display: idhā dhahabta ilā as-sūq, sa-adhhab maʿaka
variations.script: إذا ذهبت إلى السوق، سأذهب معك
variations.cue: If you go to the market, I'll go with you
variations.changed: the person in the condition: dhahabtu (I) becomes dhahabta (you-m)

mistake.display: idhā adhhab ilā as-sūq, sa-ashtarī al-khubz
mistake.script: إذا أذهب إلى السوق، سأشتري الخبز
mistake.why: This is English's "if I go" carried across word for word. idhā holds a past-shaped verb and nothing else: idhā dhahabtu ilā as-sūq.

sentences.usage: The plain open condition — a plan that depends on something, and the sentence the module's whole first half is built from.
sentences.mnemonic: idhā looks back to talk about forward.

sentences.display: idhā kunta taʿbān, lā tadhhab ilā al-ʿamal
sentences.script: إذا كنت تعبان، لا تذهب إلى العمل
sentences.cue: If you're tired, don't go to work (to a man)
sentences.literal: If you-were tired, not you-go to the-work

words.note: L1-M3's lā in front of the present-shaped verb — lā tadhhab to a man, lā tadhhabī to a woman. L2-M4's imperative idhhab has no negative at all, so lā idhhab does not exist.

sentences.trap: English builds "don't go" out of its imperative, so an English speaker reaches for idhhab and puts lā in front. Arabic switches shape entirely: the negative order is the present-tense verb, not the command.
sentences.sound: laa TADH-hab — the lā is short and leans onto the verb, exactly as it does in front of an ordinary present.

variations.display: idhā kunti taʿbāna, lā tadhhabī ilā al-ʿamal
variations.script: إذا كنت تعبانة، لا تذهبي إلى العمل
variations.cue: If you're tired, don't go to work (to a woman)
variations.changed: everything turns feminine at once: kunti, taʿbāna, lā tadhhabī

variations.display: idhā kunta taʿbān, lā taʾkul kathīran
variations.script: إذا كنت تعبان، لا تأكل كثيرًا
variations.cue: If you're tired, don't eat a lot
variations.changed: the advice: the verb behind lā becomes eating

mistake.display: idhā kunta taʿbān, lā idhhab ilā al-ʿamal
mistake.script: إذا كنت تعبان، لا اذهب إلى العمل
mistake.why: English negates its command word, so this negates idhhab. Arabic has no negative imperative: the order is given with the present-shaped verb — lā tadhhab.

sentences.usage: The module's job line in one sentence — a condition in front and advice behind it.
sentences.mnemonic: To tell someone to do it, command; to tell them not to, describe.

sentences.cue: I didn't go to school yesterday

words.note: The negative past — and the verb behind it is PRESENT-shaped, not past: lam adhhab, never lam dhahabtu. lam alone carries the time, exactly as English's "did" does.

sentences.trap: English marks the past twice over — did go — and then drops it on the second word. Arabic marks it once, on lam, and the verb stays in its present shape: lam adhhab.
sentences.sound: lam AD-hab — lam is one short clipped syllable and never takes a stress of its own.

variations.cue: I didn't drink the coffee today
variations.changed: the verb behind lam, which does not change shape for it

variations.cue: He didn't go to work yesterday
variations.changed: the person, which is still the prefix on the verb: a- becomes ya-

mistake.why: English's "didn't go" has a past somewhere in it, so a learner puts the past-tense verb behind lam. lam already is the past: lam adhhab.

sentences.usage: The everyday way to deny that something happened, and what a speaker actually says.
sentences.mnemonic: lam holds the past so the verb does not have to.

words.cue: I be (the shortened form behind lam)
words.note: L1-M6's akūn with its long vowel cut short — the jussive, and behind lam it is the only shape allowed: lam akun, lam takun, lam yakun.

sentences.trap: Nothing in English shortens here, so the vowel is what a learner keeps. akūn is the ordinary form and akun is the one lam takes, and the difference is a held vowel against a clipped one.
sentences.sound: lam A-kun — two clipped syllables in a row, and the u is short enough to nearly vanish.

variations.cue: He wasn't there yesterday
variations.changed: the person: akun (I) becomes yakun (he)

variations.cue: She wasn't busy yesterday
variations.changed: takun covers both she and you-m, and the adjective is what tells you which

mistake.why: The ordinary form kept where the jussive is wanted. This is the one place in the course a vowel length is grammar rather than spelling: lam akun.

sentences.usage: How you say you were not something — the past of the verbless sentence, which has no verb to negate otherwise.

sentences.display: lam anam ams, li-ʾannī kuntu mashghūl
sentences.script: لم أنم أمس، لأني كنت مشغول
sentences.cue: I didn't sleep yesterday, because I was busy
sentences.literal: Not I-sleep yesterday, because-I I-was busy

words.cue: I sleep (the shortened form behind lam)
words.note: L1-M9's anām with the long ā cut short, the same jussive shortening as akun. Only hollow verbs do it; lam ashrab and lam adhhab do not move at all.

sentences.trap: Two verbs with two different jobs sit side by side here: anam is shortened because lam holds it, and kuntu is an ordinary past because li-ʾannī does not.
sentences.sound: lam A-nam — three short syllables in a row, and the whole clause is over before the reason starts.

variations.display: lam yanam ams, li-ʾannahu kāna mashghūl
variations.script: لم ينم أمس، لأنه كان مشغول
variations.cue: He didn't sleep yesterday, because he was busy
variations.changed: both halves turn to he: yanam, and L1-M9's li-ʾannahu

variations.cue: I didn't sleep at night
variations.changed: the reason dropped, leaving the bare denial

mistake.why: lā denies a present or a habit — lā anām is "I don't sleep". A denial about yesterday needs the other negative: lam anam ams.

sentences.usage: A denial with its reason attached, which is L3-M3's shape running underneath a new negative.
sentences.mnemonic: lā for now, lam for then.

sentences.display: law dhahabtu ilā al-maṭʿam, la-akaltu as-samak
sentences.script: لو ذهبت إلى المطعم، لأكلت السمك
sentences.cue: If I had gone to the restaurant, I would have eaten the fish
sentences.literal: If I-went to the-restaurant, would I-ate the-fish

words.note: L2-M3's akaltu with la- glued to its front — the answer to law. That one letter is Arabic's whole conditional: there is no separate mood behind it.

sentences.trap: English needs four words for the answer — I would have eaten — and Arabic needs one letter and a past tense. Nothing else in the clause changes at all.
sentences.sound: law dha-HAB-tu … la-a-KAL-tu — law is one syllable with the aw of "how", and the la- leans forward onto its verb like sa- does.

variations.display: law kunta hunā ams, la-akalnā maʿan
variations.script: لو كنت هنا أمس، لأكلنا معًا
variations.cue: If you had been here yesterday, we would have eaten together
variations.changed: both halves turn plural at the end: la-akalnā, and L1-M10's maʿan

variations.display: law lam akun mashghūl, la-dhahabtu maʿaka
variations.script: لو لم أكن مشغول، لذهبت معك
variations.cue: If I hadn't been busy, I would have gone with you
variations.changed: the condition is negated, so lam and its shortened akun go inside law

mistake.display: law adhhab ilā al-maṭʿam, sa-ākul as-samak
mistake.script: لو أذهب إلى المطعم، سآكل السمك
mistake.why: This treats law as idhā and builds an open condition out of it. law is for what did NOT happen: past on both sides, and la- on the answer — law dhahabtu … la-akaltu.

sentences.usage: The regret sentence. It is also how a wish is said, because Arabic gives you no other frame for one.
sentences.mnemonic: law is the road not taken; la- is what was down it.

sentences.cue: I wish I had gone with you yesterday

words.cue: if only I, I wish I
words.note: One of L3-M3's sisters of anna, so the pronoun attaches for the same reason: laytanī, never layta anā. The verb behind it is past, exactly as after law.

sentences.trap: layta will not hold a free pronoun any more than anna will. The -nī on the end is the accusative M3 opened, turning up on a second particle.
sentences.sound: LAY-ta-nee — three light syllables, and the -nī at the end carries the person the way -ī does in ismī.

variations.cue: I wish I had been there
variations.changed: the verb: going becomes being, and kuntu is the past of it

variations.cue: I wish I hadn't gone
variations.changed: the wish is negated, and lam does that job inside layta

mistake.why: English says "I wish I went" with a present-looking verb and this copies the look. layta takes the past like law: laytanī dhahabtu maʿaka ams.

sentences.usage: The wish, and it is the same grammar as the regret — Arabic does not separate the two.
sentences.mnemonic: layta wears its pronoun, just as anna does.

sentences.cue: It's better that you go tomorrow

words.note: The afʿal shape of L2-M9, on the root behind ufaḍḍil: "better". min al-afḍal an is impersonal like yajibu an — nobody is named in it.

sentences.trap: English's "you'd better" has a you in it and this frame has none. The person appears only in tadhhab, at the far end of the sentence.
sentences.sound: min al-AF-ḍal an TADH-hab — the ḍ is the heavy one of min faḍlika, which is the same root doing a different job.

variations.cue: It's better that you sleep now
variations.changed: the advice, with the long ā of tanām kept because an is not lam

variations.cue: It's better that we go by train
variations.changed: the person: you becomes we, and the frame does not move

mistake.why: English pushes the person to the front — I'd better go — and this does the same. The frame is impersonal, like L3-M2's yajibu: min al-afḍal an adhhab.

sentences.usage: The gentlest advice in the module: it recommends without ordering, which is what yajibu does.
sentences.mnemonic: al-afḍal names nobody; the verb at the end does.

sentences.cue: That's good advice, thank you very much

words.note: "Advice" — countable in Arabic where English's is not, so "a good advice" is right here: naṣīḥa jayyida. n is a sun letter, so the article is an-.

sentences.trap: English has no "a" for advice and Arabic does, so hādhihi naṣīḥa is one piece of it. Counting advice is the normal thing to do here, not a mistake.
sentences.sound: na-ṢEE-ḥa — heavy ṣ in the middle and the breathy ḥ behind it, and the -a goes quiet unless a second noun follows.

variations.cue: The advice is excellent, thank you
variations.changed: the article goes on, and n assimilates it to an-

variations.cue: This is bad advice
variations.changed: the judgement flips, using L3-M3's sayyiʾa

mistake.why: naṣīḥa is feminine, so the demonstrative in front of it has to be too. English's "this" has one form and Arabic's has two: hādhihi naṣīḥa jayyida.

sentences.usage: What you say back when somebody has given you advice, and it closes the exchange politely.
sentences.mnemonic: One naṣīḥa, one piece — Arabic counts what English cannot.

sentences.display: yajibu an tanām, li-ʾanna hādhā ḍarūrī
sentences.script: يجب أن تنام، لأن هذا ضروري
sentences.cue: You must sleep, because this is necessary
sentences.literal: It-is-necessary that you-sleep, because this necessary

words.note: "Necessary" — ḍarūrī of a masculine thing, ḍarūriyya of a feminine one. It is the adjective behind L3-M2's yajibu, which is the verb of the same idea.

sentences.trap: The two ways of saying it sit in one sentence: yajibu an is the verb of necessity and ḍarūrī is the adjective. Neither needs the other, and putting a pronoun in front of yajibu is still wrong.
sentences.sound: ḍa-roo-REE — the heavy ḍ at the front, and the -ī at the end is long and stressed, not the possessive -ī of ismī.

variations.display: yajibu an tadhhab, li-ʾanna hādhā ḍarūrī
variations.script: يجب أن تذهب، لأن هذا ضروري
variations.cue: You must go, because this is necessary
variations.changed: the verb behind an, which the frame does not touch

variations.display: lā tadhhab al-yawm, hādhā laysa ḍarūrī
variations.script: لا تذهب اليوم، هذا ليس ضروري
variations.cue: Don't go today, this isn't necessary
variations.changed: the advice reverses, and L2-M7's laysa denies the adjective

mistake.display: yajibu an tanam, li-ʾanna hādhā ḍarūrī
mistake.script: يجب أن تنم، لأن هذا ضروري
mistake.why: The shortened form belongs to lam, not to an. lam tanam is right and yajibu an tanam is not: an keeps the long vowel — yajibu an tanām.

sentences.usage: The strongest advice the module gives, and the reason clause is what stops it sounding like an order.

comprehensionPool.cue: If you're hungry, I'll eat with you

comprehensionPool.script: إذا ذهبت إلى السوق، سأذهب معك

comprehensionPool.cue: It's better that you drink the water, this is necessary
This is excellent advice, thank you
